experiences/kibeho-apparitions-1981/stor:
Rwanda in 1981 was a small, densely populated and overwhelmingly Christian country, with Catholics forming the largest church. It was ruled by President Juvénal Habyarimana, and tensions between Hutu and Tutsi, rooted in colonial and post-colonial history, lay below the surface. Kibeho, in the south near the Burundi border, had a parish and a Catholic girls' secondary school, Kibeho College.

On 28 November 1981, Alphonsine Mumureke, a sixteen-year-old student, was serving in the school refectory when, she said, she heard a voice and saw a beautiful woman who called herself 'Nyina wa Jambo', Mother of the Word. At first classmates and staff mocked her and she was teased; some suspected illness. On 12 January 1982 a second student, Anathalie Mukamazimpaka, reported apparitions, and on 2 March 1982 Marie Claire Mukangango, who had been one of the most mocking students, also began to see the Virgin.

The apparitions became public events. The visionaries would fall into ecstasy before crowds of thousands, speaking with the unseen figure, sometimes singing and sometimes lying for long periods. The messages called for prayer, repentance, fasting and humility, with warnings that the world was in danger. Marie Claire was asked to spread the Rosary of the Seven Sorrows of Mary.

Observers described dramatic scenes. According to accounts collected at the time, the visionaries sometimes fell heavily to the ground during ecstasy without injury, and Alphonsine and others reported 'mystical journeys' during which they lay motionless for many hours and later described seeing places of joy and of suffering. Doctors, priests and journalists came to observe, some sympathetic, some sceptical. The messages also spoke of the world turning away from God and asked people to love one another sincerely.

The most remembered day was 15 August 1982, the feast of the Assumption. Before a large crowd, according to witnesses and later accounts, the visionaries wept and trembled and described terrifying images: rivers of blood, people killing one another, abandoned bodies without heads, trees on fire. At the time many did not understand. After the genocide of 1994, in which perhaps 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, were killed, many came to read these visions as a warning that went unheeded.

The Church moved carefully. In 1982 a medical commission and later a theological commission examined the visionaries. In 1988 Bishop Jean-Baptiste Gahamanyi of Butare authorised public devotion at Kibeho. Several others claimed visions, but these were not recognised. During the genocide Kibeho itself became a place of massacre: people who had fled to the church and school were killed in April 1994, and in April 1995 many displaced people were killed when soldiers cleared a camp at Kibeho.

Kibeho came under the new diocese of Gikongoro, led by Bishop Augustin Misago, who himself was arrested in 1999 on charges of complicity in the genocide and acquitted in 2000. On 29 June 2001 he declared that the apparitions to Alphonsine, Anathalie and Marie Claire were worthy of belief. The Sanctuary of Our Lady of Kibeho was built, and pilgrims come from Rwanda, Africa and beyond.

experiences/kibeho-apparitions-1981/sign: Kibeho is the only Catholic Marian apparition in Africa to have received official approval, and its sanctuary is a major place of pilgrimage. Its association with the 1994 genocide gives it a unique place in Rwandan memory and in reflection on the churches' responsibility during the violence. For historians and theologians it raises hard questions about prophecy read after the event, and about how Christian devotion and national tragedy were intertwined in Rwanda.
experiences/medjugorje-apparitions-1981/: Medjugorje: the 'Queen of Peace' apparitions
Podbrdo (Apparition Hill), Medjugorje, Bosnia and Herzegovina

On 24 June 1981 young people from the Croatian Catholic village of Medjugorje, then in Communist Yugoslavia, said they saw the Virgin Mary on the hill of Podbrdo. From 25 June six visionaries (Ivanka Ivanković, Mirjana Dragićević, Vicka Ivanković, Ivan Dragićević, Marija Pavlović and Jakov Čolo) reported daily apparitions, with messages calling for peace, conversion, prayer and fasting; some reported continuing apparitions for decades. The local bishops rejected the claims, the Yugoslav bishops (1991) found no proof of supernatural origin, and in 2024 the Holy See gave a 'nihil obstat' to the spiritual experience at Medjugorje without declaring the apparitions supernatural.

Many local Catholics and Franciscan friars embraced the apparitions; Communist authorities saw them as nationalist agitation and jailed the parish priest Jozo Zovko; Bishop Pavao Žanić of Mostar eventually rejected them.
Catholic (devotees)
Millions of pilgrims report conversions, confessions and healing; for them Medjugorje is a 'confessional of the world' and a true Marian call to peace.
Catholic (Holy See)

The 2024 note recognises abundant spiritual fruit and allows public devotion, but does not declare the apparitions supernatural and cautions about some messages; Pope Francis voiced scepticism about claims of daily apparitions.
Catholic (critics)
The bishops of Mostar and some theologians see the phenomenon as linked to disputes between Franciscans and the diocese, with doubts about the visionaries' consistency and continuing messages.
Protestant / Orthodox
Protestants generally reject Marian apparitions; Orthodox Christians in the region have viewed Medjugorje through the lens of Croatian-Catholic identity, especially during the 1990s wars.
Sceptical
Sceptics regard the phenomena as psychological or social, noting the long series of messages and the commercial pilgrimage economy.
Authenticity of the apparitions versus the spiritual fruits.
Franciscan-diocesan conflict in Herzegovina.
The 2024 norms and what a 'nihil obstat' means.

In 1981 Medjugorje was a poor, Croatian Catholic farming village in the hills of western Herzegovina, then part of Communist Yugoslavia. The region had a long and painful history, including violence during the Second World War. The parish was run by Franciscan friars, who had served Bosnian Catholics for centuries, and there was a long dispute between the Franciscans and the diocesan bishops of Mostar over who should run parishes.

On the afternoon of 24 June 1981, the feast of St John the Baptist, a group of young people walking near Podbrdo hill said they saw a luminous figure of a young woman holding a child. The next day, 25 June, six young people (Ivanka Ivanković, Mirjana Dragićević, Vicka Ivanković, Ivan Dragićević, Marija Pavlović and ten-year-old Jakov Čolo) went back and reported that the Virgin spoke with them. 25 June later became the anniversary date. Crowds grew rapidly, reaching thousands within days.

The authorities reacted strongly. Police questioned the young people, and doctors examined them. The Franciscan parish priest, Jozo Zovko, initially sceptical, came to support the visionaries; in August 1981 he was arrested and sentenced to prison for allegedly preaching against the state. The apparitions moved from the hill to the parish church. According to the visionaries, the Virgin identified herself as the 'Queen of Peace', calling people to peace, conversion, faith, prayer and fasting.

The local bishop, Pavao Žanić of Mostar, was initially open but later became convinced that the apparitions were not authentic, especially after the visionaries reportedly supported Franciscans in their dispute with him. His commission's negative conclusion was referred to the Yugoslav bishops' conference, which in 1991 declared at Zadar that it could not be affirmed that the events involved supernatural apparitions or revelations, while allowing pastoral care for pilgrims. Some visionaries said they still received daily or monthly messages, which continued for decades.

The visionaries also said they had been entrusted with 'secrets' about future events, which they claimed would be revealed at the proper time. Several married and raised families, some moved abroad, and they travelled widely to speak about the messages. Monthly messages, especially those reported by Marija Pavlović on the 25th of each month, were published and circulated worldwide, while critics questioned their repetitive content and the unprecedented length of the series.

Despite the official caution, Medjugorje became one of the largest Catholic pilgrimage sites in the world, drawing millions of visitors, including during and after the Bosnian war of 1992-1995. Many reported conversions, returning to confession, vocations and healings. Critics pointed to inconsistencies, commercialisation and problems in the conduct of some figures connected with the movement.

In 2010 Pope Benedict XVI established an international commission led by Cardinal Camillo Ruini, which reported in 2014. Pope Francis sent Archbishop Henryk Hoser as special envoy in 2017 and authorised official pilgrimages in 2019, while expressing personal doubts about continuing apparitions. In September 2024, under new norms, the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith issued 'The Queen of Peace', granting a nihil obstat to the spiritual experience at Medjugorje and recognising its positive fruits, but explicitly without declaring the apparitions supernatural.

Medjugorje is the most visited and most controversial Marian site of modern times, shaping Catholic devotion, pilgrimage and renewal movements worldwide. The long Church process around it, from local rejection to a 2024 nihil obstat without recognition of supernatural origin, illustrates the Catholic Church's evolving approach to private revelation. It also shows how apparitions become entangled in local church disputes, national identities and global religious tourism.
